q: Inside the city limits of Nice, vine terraces climbing toward 300 metres carry Braquet and Folle Noire, grapes hardly grown anywhere else in France. Name the appellation.
exp: The terraces hang above the Var valley at the back of the city, high enough that the wines stay light and perfumed through a Riviera summer. Braquet makes a pale, strawberry-scented rose and Folle Noire a firm, dark red, Rolle carries the whites, and nearly all of it is drunk in the restaurants of Nice itself.

q: Merlot and Chardonnay with the grape named on the front label built the Midi's export revival. What does IGP Pays d'Oc offer that the appellations of the hills do not?
opts: Freedom from any yield limit at all
The right to buy finished wine from anywhere in France and blend it in
An exemption from every analysis and tasting control
Varietal labels, and grapes the appellation decrees shut out
exp: The IGP is where varietal labelling and the international varieties live: Chardonnay has an appellation home at Limoux, while Merlot and Cabernet reach the appellation map only in the Atlantic-facing blends of Cabardes and Malepere, so a wine sold on its grape name needs the IGP either way. Nearly every other appellation works from a fixed Mediterranean variety list, and one region runs two wine economies side by side.

q: Down where the Pyrenees drop into the sea, Grenache fermented dry rather than muted goes out as Collioure, once a red alone. Which colours may the label claim today?
opts: Red, rose or white alike
Red or rose, but never white
Red or white, but never rose
Red only, as at the start
exp: The red dates from 1971, the rose followed, and the white joined the decree in 2002, built on Grenache Blanc and Gris. The vineyard is the same terraced schist the sweet wine is drawn from, and a grower decides vat by vat whether to ferment dry or to mute, so one terrace can end the year under either name.

q: Selling in bulk to a bottler outside the denomination keeps that wine out of Spain's highest tier for good. Which requirement shuts that door?
opts: Wine at the qualified tier may be sold only inside Spain
Wine at the qualified tier must age two years before release
Wine at the qualified tier must be bottled inside the delimited zone
Wine at the qualified tier must be pressed within a day of picking
exp: Bottling at origin is the point of the rung: once a tanker leaves the zone the regulating body has no way of knowing what reaches the glass, so the qualified tier simply refuses to let it go. Wine may still change hands in bulk between registered bodegas inside the boundary, which is how growers and cooperatives supply the ageing houses, but the last stop before the cork has to be a registered cellar in the zone. The condition falls hardest on houses whose business was built on selling wine by the litre to a bottler somewhere else, which is much of why so few denominations have ever applied.

q: A back label carries the mark of Grandes Pagos de Espana, and a guest reads it as a rank above DO. What is it really?
opts: The top rung of the national quality ladder
A seal issued by each denomination's regulating body after a compulsory tasting of every lot
A private association of estates, admitted by its own members
A denomination covering single estates in Castilla-La Mancha
exp: Nothing in Spanish wine law mentions it; the estates set their own standards and vote on who joins, which is a guild rather than a rank. It is worth knowing precisely because the wording sits so close to the legal single-estate category that a guest cannot be expected to tell them apart.

q: An estate already holding Spain's single-property denomination happens to lie inside the boundary of a qualified region, and its category picks up an extra word. Give the full name.
accept: denominacion de origen de pago calificado
exp: The law provides for it directly: a pago sitting within a qualified denomination, and meeting that denomination's requirements as well as its own, takes the longer name. It is the only place in the Spanish system where two categories are stacked on one bottle, and there are barely a handful of estates it can apply to at all.

q: Three new rungs went into Rioja's rulebook in 2017, ranking ground instead of counting months in cask. Which set of names is right?
opts: Vino de Pago, Vino de Villa and Vina Clasificada
Crianza de Zona, Reserva de Municipio and Vinedo Historico
Vino de Paraje, Vino de Pueblo and Gran Vinedo
Vino de Zona, Vino de Municipio and Vinedo Singular
exp: The ladder narrows from one of the three zones, to a named town, to a single plot, and it runs alongside the ageing words rather than replacing them, so a bottle can carry a village name and Reserva at once. It was a deliberate answer to the charge that Rioja ranked cellars and not vineyards, and it borrows its shape openly from Burgundy.

q: A white Rioja lists Tempranillo Blanco on its back label, and the guest assumes a research station bred it. Where did the variety actually come from?
opts: A crossing of Tempranillo and Viura made at a Logrono research station
A Bordeaux white brought south during the phylloxera years
An old white recovered from abandoned plots and identified by DNA
A single mutated shoot found on a Tempranillo vine in a Rioja vineyard
exp: A grower found one arm of an ordinary black Tempranillo bearing white berries, and the shoot was propagated, tested and eventually written into the rulebook. Rioja authorised it in 2007 in a batch of nine varieties that took in Maturana Blanca and Turruntes alongside Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and Verdejo, so the same reform bought native identity and international insurance at one stroke.

q: Fruit off a young plot cannot go into Rioja's single-vineyard bottling however good the wine turns out. How old must the vines be?
accept: the vines must be thirty five years old
a minimum of thirty five years
at least thirty five years old
vines at least thirty five years old
a minimum of thirty five years old
exp: The tier also demands hand harvesting, a yield well below the general limit, and a pass in two separate tastings before the back label is released. Age alone was never going to be enough on its own, because a mediocre old plot is easy to find, but it is the condition that cannot be met by simply farming better next year.

q: Rioja lets a label name a zone only when the fruit comes wholly from it, and the cellar steps must happen inside that same zone as well. Name the one that comes first.
accept: the wine must be vinified there
the wine must be vinified in the zone
it must be vinified in the zone
the wine has to be made in the zone
the wine must be made in the zone
it must be made in the zone
must be made in the zone
exp: A winery outside the boundary cannot print the zone even if every grape came from inside it, which stops a name being attached to fruit trucked anywhere convenient. Vinification is only the first step the rule catches, since the ageing and the bottling have to happen inside the zone as well. That is why the zone names took so long to appear on labels at all, plenty of established bodegas drawing fruit from more than one of the three.

q: Whole bunches go uncrushed into an open stone lagar in an Alavesa village, and the wine is sold off before the next vintage comes in. What is a wine made that way called?
exp: The bunches ferment under their own weight, partly inside the intact berries, and the wine goes into bottle purple, low in tannin and meant for the winter. It is the oldest commercial style in Rioja and it survived the whole barrel-ageing era in the villages, which is why it turns up in Alavesa bars and almost nowhere on an export list.

q: A Spanish white has spent four years ageing, six months of that in barrel. Which of the ladder's words may the bodega print?
opts: None of them, the ladder having been written for red wine alone
Gran Reserva
Crianza, because only six of the forty-eight months were spent in wood
Reserva, that word being the highest a white may reach
exp: The white and rosado timetable is shorter than the red one at every rung, and its wood requirement is much lighter: four years in all with six months in cask carries the top word. A red asking for the same word needs five years, and far more of them in oak, which is why a white Gran Reserva costs a fraction of what its name suggests.

q: Spain's national rulebook asks a red Gran Reserva for sixty months of ageing in all, and fixes a floor for the share of it that must pass in oak. Give that floor.
accept: at least eighteen months in oak
at least eighteen months in cask
exp: Sixty months in all, at least eighteen of them in an oak cask, is the whole of what the national text asks of a red at the top rung. A denomination may set a harder rule for its own producers and the serious ones have, so the word compares cleanly only inside a single rulebook: two bottles both reading Gran Reserva can differ by a year or more of wood. What is being measured either way is elapsed time and nothing else, which is why the rung says nothing at all about where the fruit grew.

q: Spain's ageing words name two places and no third, so a bodega that leaves its Reserva a year in stainless steel gains nothing by it. Which two places?
accept: ageing in cask and in bottle
aging in cask and in bottle
in cask and in bottle only
exp: Both clocks run at once inside a single total, so a rule reading thirty-six months with twelve in cask leaves the remainder to be served in glass. Steel is named nowhere in the definitions, so a bodega holding stock in tank earns neither cask time nor bottle time towards Reserva or Gran Reserva. Crianza is the one loose thread, its definition fixing the total and the cask floor but never saying where the balance must sit, so at that rung alone the months out of the barrel may pass in tank.

q: Reserva asks less of a white than of a red, a full year less in fact. Give the white's total under the national rule.
accept: a minimum of twenty four months
exp: Twenty-four months for a white or rosado against thirty-six for a red, and the white needs only six of them in cask. The gap runs the whole length of the ladder, so every one of the three words means something different depending on the colour of what is in the bottle.

q: Old plots around Toro carry untrellised bush vines set very wide apart and never watered. Which constraint dictated that layout?
opts: A denomination rule capping the vines that may be registered on a hectare
The shallow water table, which every root reaches within a metre of the surface
The risk of spring frost, which settles more heavily in a trellised canopy
The low rainfall, which leaves each vine a wide patch to itself
exp: Toro takes little more than a third of a metre of rain in a year, so the vineyard is spaced to the water rather than to the tractor. The same arithmetic explains the goblet: a low free-standing head shades its own fruit and needs no wire, posts and wire being an expense that pays only where there is enough water to grow a canopy worth training.
